title: Type I and Type II Error

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A Type I error is rejecting H₀ when it is true: concluding there is an effect when there is none. A Type II error is failing to reject H₀ when it is false: missing an effect that exists.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A test is a decision made from one sample, so it can go wrong in two ways. Cross the two true states (H₀ true, H₀ false) with the two decisions (reject, do not reject) and you get a 2 × 2 table:

Decision H₀ true H₀ false
Reject H₀ Type I error (probability α) Correct (probability 1 − β, the power)
Do not reject H₀ Correct (probability 1 − α) Type II error (probability β)

Figure 8.1 draws the two columns as two sampling distributions of the urban–rural difference, both with SE = 0.406 kg (recall §7.2.3). If H₀ is true, the observed difference centres on 0. If the true difference is 1 kg, it centres on 1. A two-sided test at α = 0.05 rejects H₀ when the observed difference lies beyond ±1.96 × 0.406 = ±0.80 kg. The red tails are the Type I error: the chance, under H₀, of landing beyond the cut-offs. The grey area is the Type II error: the chance, when the truth is 1 kg, of landing inside them.

blocks.alt: Two normal curves of the observed urban–rural difference, centred at 0 kg (H₀) and 1 kg (H₁), with critical values at ±0.80 kg; the H₀ tails beyond them are shaded as Type I error and the H₁ area between them as Type II error.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.1. Type I and Type II error for the urban–rural comparison of §7.2.3 (SE 0.406 kg). Two-sided test at α = 0.05: α/2 = 0.025 in each tail of the H₀ curve; β = 0.31 under a true 1 kg difference, so power = 0.69.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Testing a new drug against H₀ “no effect”: a Type I error means approving a useless drug; a Type II error means abandoning a useful one. The two errors often differ in cost, which is why the choice of α (§8.4) is a judgement, not a law. Move the cut-offs in Figure 8.1 outwards (a smaller α) and the red tails shrink while the grey area grows.

points.html: α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true); β = P(do not reject H₀ | H₀ false). 1 − β is the power (§8.4).

For a fixed sample size and design, lowering α raises β. To lower both you must shrink the standard error. For a given design and variability the main lever is sample size (SE falls with √n, recall §6.7). A paired or matched design, or a more precise measurement, also lowers the SE and so reduces both errors.
β is not one number: it depends on the true effect. In Figure 8.1, β = 0.31 for a true 1 kg difference; for a true 0.5 kg difference it is larger (§8.4).
